items.title: Constantinople fell to Ottoman cannons in 1453

options.text: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople from 6 April; massive Hungarian-built cannons breached the Theodosian walls; the city fell on 29 May 1453, ending the 1,123-year Eastern Roman Empire

items.reveal:
Mehmed II, aged 21, had artillery cast by Orban, a Hungarian engineer — including the Basilic, around 8 metres long, firing stone balls of around 270 kg. The walls of Theodosius (built 5th century) had held for a thousand years; gunpowder ended their effectiveness.

Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos died in the fighting; his body was never identified. Around 7,000 Byzantine and Genoese defenders faced perhaps 80,000-150,000 Ottoman troops.

Mehmed converted Hagia Sophia into a mosque (it remained one until 1934, when Atatürk converted it to a museum; reconverted to a mosque in 2020). The fall pushed Greek scholars and texts west into Italy — fuel for the late Renaissance.
items.why: Military technology can end empires. The fall of Constantinople closes the medieval Mediterranean and marks a conventional boundary between medieval and early modern history.

items.title: Henry VII was a 'modern' monarch — by destroying the nobility
items.claim: How did Henry VII (r. 1485-1509) consolidate power?

options.text: By distributing land widely among loyal nobles
By using bonds and recognisances to financially bind nobles, the Star Chamber to bypass juries, and avoiding war to keep crown finances strong
By creating a standing army of 50,000 men
By moving the capital from London to York

items.reveal:
Henry VII forced nobles to enter bonds — written debts payable to the crown on bad behaviour. By 1509 around two-thirds of the peerage was under bond. Empson and Dudley managed crown revenue ruthlessly.

The Star Chamber, sitting at Westminster, dealt with cases the common-law courts could not — overmighty nobles intimidating juries. Henry VII left £1.5 million in the treasury (his son spent it in a decade). He fought one continental war.
items.why: Henry VII is the boring Tudor — but his fiscal-administrative state is what makes Henry VIII's ambition possible. Modern bureaucratic monarchy starts here, not at the Reformation.

items.title: The Glorious Revolution was a Dutch invasion
items.claim: William of Orange landed in Devon on 5 November 1688. How large was the force?

options.text: A diplomatic mission of a few hundred men
Around 15,000 troops on 463 ships — larger than the Spanish Armada
Only James II's English defectors, no foreign troops
A small English army recruited in advance by Parliament

items.reveal:
Seven English nobles (the 'Immortal Seven') invited William in June 1688. He landed at Brixham, Devon, with 15,000-21,000 Dutch troops, plus thousands of horses and 50 cannon. James II's army melted; key officers (including John Churchill, the future Duke of Marlborough) defected.

James fled to France in December. The Convention Parliament (January 1689) declared the throne vacant and offered it to William and Mary. The Bill of Rights followed in December 1689.

The Williamite War in Ireland (Boyne 1690) and the Highland war in Scotland (Killiecrankie 1689) were anything but bloodless.
items.why: The 'Glorious Revolution' as bloodless English self-determination is a Whig myth. It was a foreign-backed coup with extensive bloodshed in Ireland and Scotland — successful, but not peaceful.
